readerTitle: The restaurant that hit its goal and got worse
caseNote: 가상 사례 (비스트로, 구독 앱) + 실제 연구 (Ordóñez 외 2009, Locke & Latham 2002) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 목표는 방향을 정해 줄 뿐이고 결과를 만드는 것은 매일 반복하는 시스템이다. 그래서 목표를 세운 뒤에는 '평범한 화요일에 무엇이 달라지는가'를 물어야 한다.
misconception: 목표를 높고 분명하게 세우고 보상을 걸면 성과는 따라온다. 목표 숫자를 달성했다면 사업이 나아진 것이다.

sources.text: Ordóñez, L. D., Schweitzer, M. E., Galinsky, A. D., & Bazerman, M. H. (2009). Goals Gone Wild: The Systematic Side Effects of Overprescribing Goal Setting. Academy of Management Perspectives, 23(1), 6–16.
Locke, E. A., & Latham, G. P. (2002). Building a Practically Useful Theory of Goal Setting and Task Motivation. American Psychologist, 57(9), 705–717.
비스트로와 구독 앱 사례, 별점 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Ordóñez 외(2009)의 주장 요약(좁은 목표는 측정되지 않는 부분을 소홀히 하게 하고, 위험 감수와 편법을 늘릴 수 있다)이 논문 내용과 맞는지 게시 전에 원문으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 연구 수치를 쓰지 않고 주장만 일반적으로 적었습니다.
Locke & Latham의 '구체적이고 어려운 목표가 막연한 목표보다 성과를 높인다'는 요약이 2002년 논문 결론과 일치하는지 확인하세요.
비스트로 별점 4.2 → 4.8 → 4.3과 6주, 가을 등 시점은 모두 가상 수치입니다. 계산이 필요한 수치는 없습니다.

cards.title: The restaurant that hit its goal and got worse
body: A neighborhood bistro sat at 4.2 stars online. The owner set a clear goal: 4.7 by summer, with a bonus for the team if they made it.
They reached 4.8 in six weeks. By autumn the rating was back at 4.3, and two good cooks had quit. Nothing about the food had changed.

image.label: A rating sign rising, then sliding back down
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 작은 비스트로 창문에 별점 그래프가 붙어 있고, 선이 4.2에서 4.8로 급히 올랐다가 4.3으로 미끄러져 내려옴. 주방 안 요리사는 그대로 바쁘게 일하는 모습. 실제 리뷰 사이트 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your reviews are stuck at 4.2.
body: You own a 40-seat bistro. Reviews mention slow mains on busy nights and the odd cold plate. You want a better reputation this year.
What's your first move?

options.text: Set a target of 4.7 stars by June and pay a team bonus if you hit it
options.feedback: Clear and motivating, but it rewards the number, not the meal. People will find the fastest way to move the rating, and that may not be better food.

options.text: Ask servers to invite happy tables to leave a review
options.feedback: It lifts the rating quickly and costs little. But it only changes who writes reviews, so the slow mains and cold plates are still there.

options.text: Fix the routine behind the top complaint: a pass check before every plate and a second cook on Friday nights
options.feedback: Slower to show up in the rating, and it costs labor. But it changes what guests actually get, every night, whether anyone is watching the score or not.

cards.title: The number moved. The bistro didn't.
body: In our story the owner chose A. Servers asked only the happiest tables for reviews. A few offered free desserts in return. Hosts steered regulars to the busiest nights to post.
The rating jumped. But the kitchen ran exactly as before. When the bonus ended, so did the review drive, and the old complaints came back into view.
Everyone worked hard. They just worked on the score instead of on the restaurant.

cards.title: Goals vs systems
body: A **goal** is the result you want: 4.7 stars, $1 million in sales, a faster checkout. A **system** is what you do over and over that produces results: the daily routines, checks and habits.

Here's the catch. Every restaurant on the street wants great reviews. The goal doesn't separate them. What separates them is the system: how plates are checked, how busy nights are staffed, how complaints get fixed.

image.label: A flag on a hill versus the steps that lead up to it
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 언덕 꼭대기에 "Goal: 4.7 stars" 깃발. 오른쪽에 깃발로 이어지는 계단, 계단마다 "Pass check", "Friday second cook", "Weekly complaint review" 라벨. 계단 쪽을 더 밝고 크게 강조.

cards.title: Goals work, and they also have side effects.
body: Decades of research by Edwin Locke and Gary Latham found that specific, hard goals usually beat vague ones like "do your best." Goals focus effort.

But in a 2009 paper, *Goals Gone Wild*, Lisa Ordóñez and colleagues argued that focus cuts both ways. Narrow goals can make people ignore what isn't measured, take bigger risks and cut corners to hit the number.
Both can be true. A goal points effort somewhere. The system decides whether that effort builds anything.

cards.title: What changes on an ordinary Tuesday?
body: Take any goal and ask: if we're serious, what will we do differently on a normal day? If the answer is "try harder," you have a wish, not a plan.

A bakery that wants more repeat customers might change nothing at all, or it might start a rule: every regular gets greeted by name, and the bestsellers never run out before noon. The second version will still be running long after the goal is forgotten.
cards.softwareNote: A product team aiming for 10,000 signups can hit it with one big launch push. A team that talks to five users and ships one fix every week builds something that keeps users coming back after the push ends.

cards.title: Systems without goals drift.
body: This isn't a case against goals. A routine with no target can run for years without anyone checking whether it works. The goal is how you know.

So use both. Let the goal choose the system, then judge the system by the goal over months, not weeks. Good systems are slower to show results, and a short deadline can make a shortcut look better than it is.
And watch what a bonus rewards. If it pays for the number alone, expect the number alone.

cards.title: Now it's a subscription app.
body: You lead a team at a meal-planning app. Too many users cancel in their second month. The board wants churn, the share of subscribers who leave each month, cut sharply by next quarter.
What do you put in place?

options.text: Set the churn target, tie it to team bonuses and let them figure it out
options.feedback: Clear ownership, but no routine for finding the cause. Expect quick fixes that move the number and leave the reason people leave untouched.

options.text: Show a 50% discount to everyone who clicks cancel
options.feedback: It will cut churn fast, and it hides the problem behind lower prices. You keep users but earn less from each, and they may still leave later.

options.text: Every week, talk to five users who cancelled, fix the most common reason, and review churn monthly
options.feedback: Slower and less dramatic. But it's a routine that keeps finding and removing reasons to leave, and the churn target tells you whether it's working.

cards.title: Goals set the direction. Systems do the work.
body: Hitting a number isn't the same as getting better. Judge a goal by the routine it changes, then judge the routine by the goal over time.
**Try it today:** pick one goal you're chasing. Write down one thing your team will now do every day or every week because of it. If you can't, start there.
